title: Max your 401(k) / 403(b) employee contribution
summary: $24,500 employee deferral for 2026, with catch-up provisions at 50+ and a super catch-up at 60–63.
detailsHtml:
2026 limits

Standard: $24,500 Catch-up (50+): $32,500 (+$8,000) Super catch-up (ages 60–63): $35,750 (+$11,250)

The super catch-up

Under SECURE 2.0, workers ages 60–63 can make enhanced catch-up contributions of $11,250 instead of the standard $8,000 — a window designed for last-decade-of-career acceleration. Returns to $8,000 at age 64.

New for 2026 — high-earner Roth catch-up requirement (with transition relief): Under SECURE 2.0 §603, if your prior-year (2025) FICA wages exceeded $150,000, age-50+ catch-up contributions must be made as Roth, not pre-tax. However, the final regulations issued November 17, 2025 set mandatory plan compliance for plan years beginning after December 31, 2026 — meaning many plans are using transition relief through 2026 and continuing to accept pre-tax catch-ups. As of mid-2026, roughly 80% of large employer plans have Roth catch-up operational; smaller plans are running closer to 50% adoption. Check with your plan administrator before assuming you're locked out of catch-up. By 2027 plan years, plans without Roth capability will have to either add it or stop accepting age-50+ catch-up from high earners.
${bracketBlock( 'You may prefer Roth 401(k) here, but the case for prioritizing the IRA over additional 401(k) contributions (point 6.2) is weaker for you, since your 12% bracket means the tax deduction from Traditional contributions is small. Roth 401(k) at this stage is reasonable.', 'Split between Roth and Traditional based on your retirement bracket projection. Many in this range default to Traditional and use the tax savings to either fund a Roth IRA or build a taxable account for early-retirement bridge capital.', 'Strongly prefer Traditional 401(k). The deduction is worth 32–37 cents per dollar contributed. The future tax rate would have to be higher than the current rate for Roth to win, and most high earners drop to 22–24% in retirement.' )}
